title: Esports Governance Case Challenge
intro: You’re advising an esports organization. Review each case, identify who has authority, and explain what makes the decision accountable.
instructions: Four case files, seven multiple-choice questions, and one short recommendation
10 points total; plan for about 10–12 minutes
You may consult the posted slides and assigned chapter. Base your answers on the materials.
You may revise your work before your one final submission.

cases.title: One incident, two authorities
cases.subtitle: Valve, ESIC, and the CS:GO spectator bug
evidence: Coaches exploited a camera bug to gain an unfair view during matches.
ESIC investigated and issued findings and sanctions. Valve announced its own Major-eligibility schedule in January 2021.
Use the historical schedule below for this case; it is not a statement of every current competition rule.

questions.prompt: A coach receives four ESIC demerits. Under Valve’s displayed schedule, what consequence should you advise the team to expect?

options.text: Exclusion from four Majors
Exclusion from all future Majors
Exclusion from three Majors
Exclusion from two Majors

questions.prompt: A team manager says, “Once ESIC sanctioned the coach, Valve had no separate decision to make.” Which response best matches this case?

options.text: Valve used ESIC’s findings to impose consequences within Valve’s own competition scope.
Valve’s schedule replaced ESIC’s sanctions in every competition covered by ESIC.
ESIC’s investigation transferred Major-eligibility decisions from Valve to individual organizers.
Valve acted as an appeals tribunal that reviewed whether ESIC had correctly decided the case.

cases.title: Warning signs and a reporting duty
cases.subtitle: Nyamdorj v. ESIC
evidence: Counter-Strike player Tuvshintugs “Annihilation” Nyamdorj appealed a 12-month ESIC sanction.
His letter described recurring unexplained gameplay decisions and underperformance. He characterized it as team dysfunction; ESIC argued it showed integrity concerns.
IGET reviewed the disciplinary decision and ESIC’s request to increase the sanction.

questions.prompt: You are advising a participant about the reporting rule applied in Nyamdorj. Which statement best describes its trigger?

options.text: The participant may wait until an organizer confirms that a match was manipulated.
The duty begins only when the participant knows which person personally profited.
The participant must prove the underlying corruption before making a report.
Facts that may evidence corruption can trigger reporting before certainty or proof exists.

questions.prompt: Which description accurately explains how independent review operated in Nyamdorj?

options.text: IGET overturned the sanction because the evidence did not establish personal profit.
IGET upheld 12 months but rejected ESIC’s proposed increase to 24 months.
IGET increased the sanction because challenging ESIC automatically removed any discount.
IGET replaced the reporting finding with a finding of active match-fixing.

cases.title: A publisher goes to court
cases.subtitle: Epic Games Inc. v. Araujo
evidence: Epic alleged repeated Fortnite cheating and evasion of its bans using false accounts and hardware tools.
It pursued civil claims involving anti-circumvention law, contract, and copyright.
Araujo did not appear or defend. The court entered a default judgment, awarded civil relief, and imposed a permanent injunction.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes Epic’s civil lawsuit from its internal decision to ban a player?

options.text: A court must adopt the publisher’s rulebook as the controlling law for every claim.
A court becomes the publisher’s routine appeals panel for all eligibility decisions.
The publisher must establish a legal basis for the judicial relief it requests.
An internal ban establishes entitlement to any damages the publisher requests.

questions.prompt: A colleague says, “Araujo defaulted, so the court had to accept every legal conclusion and remedy Epic requested.” What is the best correction?

options.text: The court accepted well-pleaded facts but still evaluated legal sufficiency and relief.
The court had to retry the entire dispute as if both parties had presented evidence.
The court could enforce a competition ban but could not award civil damages.
The court could award damages without considering whether the claims were legally sufficient.

cases.title: The governance audit
cases.subtitle: Your recommendation to a fictional league
evidence: A fictional esports league promises participants “fair treatment.”
Its rules do not identify who hears appeals or require written reasons for disciplinary decisions.
The league director asks you to recommend one specific governance improvement.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is best supported by these facts?

options.text: The league has demonstrated accountability because its rules promise fair treatment.
The league lacks any authority to discipline participants because it is a private body.
The league must transfer every dispute to IGET because its own rules omit an appeal process.
The fairness promise lacks specified procedures for explaining and reviewing decisions.

writing.prompt: For the fictional league in Case File 4, recommend one specific change. Identify the governance gap your change addresses, describe a workable safeguard, and name who must implement it. Explain how the change would make the league accountable.
